    - text: Problem (x³ + 0x² + 0x − 1) ÷ (x − 1) Quotient x² + x + 1 x − 1
    - strong: x³ + 0x² + 0x − 1
    - article:
      - text: − (x³ − x² + 0x + 0)
      - separator
      - text: 0x³ + x² + 0x − 1
    - article:
      - text: − (0x³ + x² − x + 0)
      - separator
      - text: 0x³ + 0x² + x − 1
    - article:
      - text: − (0x³ + 0x² + x − 1)
      - separator
      - text: 0x³ + 0x² + 0x + 0
    - text: Remainder 0
    - complementary:
      - img
      - text: Failing to insert zero coefficients misaligns terms.
    - complementary:
      - heading "Identity Check ⓘ" [level=2]
      - paragraph: Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder
      - text: LHS (Dividend) x³ + 0x² + 0x − 1
      - strong: =
      - text: RHS (x − 1)(x² + x + 1) + 0
      - paragraph: Expand RHS
      - text: (x − 1)(x² + x + 1) + 0 LHS = RHS
      - img
      - text: Identity verified
      - heading "Rules" [level=2]
      - paragraph: • Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder
      - paragraph: • deg(Remainder) < deg(Divisor)
    - article:
      - heading "Why It Works" [level=2]
      - paragraph: At each step we cancel the leading term of the current dividend using the divisor.
      - paragraph: Each subtraction reduces the degree of the remaining polynomial until the degree is less than the divisor's degree.
      - text: Highest degree term → cancel → degree drops → stop
      - img
    - article:
      - heading "Worked Example ✓ Verified" [level=2]
      - paragraph: Divide (x³ − 1) by (x − 1).
      - paragraph: "Quotient: x² + x + 1"
      - paragraph: "Remainder: 0"
      - paragraph: "Check: (x − 1)(x² + x + 1) + 0 = x³ − 1"

    - heading "Common Misconception" [level=2]:
      - img
      - text: Common Misconception
    - paragraph: Skipping zero coefficients causes misalignment of like terms and wrong results.
    - article: ✕ Incorrect (skips zero terms) (x³ − 1) ÷ (x − 1)
    - article: ✓ Correct (include zeros) x³ + 0x² + 0x − 1
    - complementary:
      - text: Why it matters
      - paragraph: Zero coefficients keep all powers aligned so each subtraction cancels the leading term properly.
